manuallyAdjudicatedChangedSelection.recognizedQuestion: five replicas initially store tag zero and value zero one writer assigns increasing integer tags sends each tagged value to all replicas and completes after three acknowledgements replicas retain only the highest tag received a reader queries any three replicas and returns the highest tagged value without writing back messages may be delayed arbitrarily replicas do not fail is this register linearizable give an explicit execution proving your answer naming replicas and operation ordering then determine whether making each reader write its selected tagged value to three replicas before returning restores linearizability including with concurrent readers and an unfinished write prove your conclusion
manuallyAdjudicatedChangedSelection.answer:
No. Without read write-back, successive reads can return a new value and then an old one. Write-back restores linearizability if the reader waits for acknowledgements from three distinct replicas before returning—not merely sends the messages.

Name the replicas A, B, C, D and E; initially each stores (0, 0).
1. W1 starts writing (1, 10). Deliver it only to A, which stores it and acknowledges. Delay delivery to B–E, so W1 remains unfinished.
2. R1 queries {A, B, C}, receives (1, 10), (0, 0), (0, 0), and returns 10.
3. After R1 returns, R2 starts and queries {B, D, E}. All three still store (0, 0), so R2 returns 0.

This is not linearizable: R1 returning 10 requires placing W1 before R1. Real-time order places R1 before R2, so with no other write, R2 cannot return 0. Leaving W1 unfinished does not resolve that contradiction.

With write-back, R1 must propagate (1, 10), for example to {A, B, C}, and receive all three acknowledgements before returning. R2’s quorum {B, D, E} intersects that completed write-back at B, so R2 must select tag at least 1. This repairs the step where R1 previously returned without establishing a quorum containing its selected tag.

Here is the general proof. Assume tags uniquely identify writes and increase in writer order; replicas update monotonically and acknowledge only after retaining a tag at least as large as the received tag. Every completed write or read establishes a three-replica quorum holding tags at least its own. Any read invoked afterward queries an intersecting quorum, so it selects a tag no smaller. A write invoked afterward also has a larger tag: every tag seen by a read originated in an already-invoked write.

Order writes by tag, and put each read immediately after the write whose tag it returns, before any higher-tag write; order equal-tag reads consistently with real time. The quorum argument ensures this ordering respects every completed-before-invoked relationship. A read cannot return a tag from a write invoked after that read completed, because tags are not invented. These facts establish a legal sequential register history.

Concurrent readers may select different tags; an older reader’s delayed write-back cannot overwrite a newer tag. If a read observes an unfinished write, include that pending write in the linearized history before the read. The writer need not actually finish: the reader’s acknowledged write-back establishes the quorum needed for subsequent reads. This
